n: A good reputation is worth more than great wealth, and being well thought of is better than silver or gold.
Rich and poor share one thing: the Lord made them both. Every person has equal worth before God.

f.w: the LORD is the maker of them all

n: The prudent see danger coming and take cover; the naive keep going and pay for it.

f.w: A prudent man foreseeth the evil

n: Humility and reverence for the Lord bring riches, honor, and life.
Thorns and traps line the road of the crooked; those who guard their lives stay far away.

A beloved promise to parents: teach a child well and that training tends to last a lifetime. It is a general principle, not a guarantee—children have agency—but early teaching has deep, lasting influence.

f.g: Train = dedicate, start off; possibly “according to his way,” suited to the child.

f.w: when he is old, he will not depart from it

n: An honest observation about money: the rich rule over the poor, and borrowers become servants to lenders. A strong caution against debt.

f.w: the borrower is servant to the lender

n: Whoever sows injustice will reap disaster, and the rod he used in anger will be broken.

f.w: He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity

n: A generous person will be blessed because he shares his food with the poor.

f.g: Literally “a good eye”—a generous, kindly outlook.

n: Remove the mocker and quarrels leave with him; strife and insults stop.
Whoever loves a pure heart and speaks graciously will have the king as a friend.
The Lord watches over true knowledge but frustrates the words of the treacherous.

f.w: The eyes of the LORD preserve knowledge

n: A humorous excuse: the lazy person won’t go out to work because “there’s a lion outside!” Any excuse will do.
The adulteress’s mouth is a deep pit, and those under God’s displeasure fall into it.

f.g: abhorred = regarded with disgust; under God’s wrath.

n: Children naturally have foolishness bound up in them, and loving discipline helps drive it away. The “rod” stands for correction; the gospel calls for discipline given with love and gentleness.
Oppressing the poor to get rich, or giving gifts to the rich to win favor, both lead to poverty.

A new collection, “the words of the wise,” begins here and runs to 24:22. Many scholars note similarities between it and an Egyptian wisdom text, the Instruction of Amenemope. It opens with a call to listen.

f.g: A heading for a new section of the book (22:17–24:22).

n: It’s good to keep these sayings in your heart and have them ready on your lips.

f.g: withal = together, at the same time.

n: The purpose of these teachings: that your trust will be in the Lord. Wisdom is ultimately about faith.

f.w: That thy trust may be in the LORD

n: The teacher asks: haven’t I written for you excellent sayings of counsel and knowledge? Some translate “thirty sayings,” matching Amenemope’s thirty chapters.

f.g: The Hebrew may read “thirty sayings,” a possible structural note for this section.

n: These teachings give you confidence in what is true, so you can bring back reliable answers to those who sent you.

f.w: the certainty of the words of truth

n: Don’t exploit the poor because they are weak, or crush the needy in court. The gate was where legal cases were judged.

f.g: The city gate, where elders heard legal cases.

n: The Lord himself will take up the case of the poor and will plunder those who plundered them.

f.w: the LORD will plead their cause

n: Don’t make friends with a hot-tempered person or spend time with someone easily angered.

f.w: Make no friendship with an angry man

n: You might pick up his habits and get yourself trapped.
Don’t be one who shakes hands to guarantee other people’s debts.

f.g: Shake hands to seal a pledge.

n: If you can’t pay, even your bed may be taken from under you. Co-signing puts your basic necessities at risk.
Don’t move the ancient boundary stones your ancestors set. Moving them was a sneaky way to steal land.

f.g: Boundary stones marking a family’s inherited land.

n: Do you see someone skilled at their work? They will serve kings, not obscure people. Excellence opens doors—as with Joseph and Daniel.
